d: The heaviest invertebrate known, with swivelling hooks on its arms; first filmed alive (a juvenile) in 2025.
x: Overview # Shorter but much heavier than the giant squid. Its arm and tentacle clubs carry rotating hooks as well as suckers. Habitat and type of water # Southern Ocean around Antarctica. Feeding and hunting # Thought to be an ambush predator because of its slow metabolism. It preys on Patagonian and Antarctic toothfish. Mating and reproduction # Poorly known. Females produce many eggs. Movement and migration # Juveniles live shallower and adults deeper. Behaviour and social life # A main prey of sperm whales in the Southern Ocean. Adaptations # Swivelling hooks Huge eyes Ammonium-based buoyancy Conservation # Rarely encountered. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colossal_squid WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Mesonychoteuthis%20hamiltoni FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Mesonychoteuthis%20hamiltoni

d: The deepest-living octopuses, flapping ear-like fins; one was filmed at nearly 7,000 m.
x: Overview # Cirrate octopuses with fins on their mantle and finger-like cirri along their arms. They swallow prey whole. Habitat and type of water # Worldwide, bathyal to hadal depths. Feeding and hunting # Hovers above the seafloor and pounces on crustaceans and worms, swallowing them whole. Mating and reproduction # Females carry eggs at various stages and lay them on hard substrates when conditions suit. There is no fixed breeding season. Movement and migration # Little horizontal movement. Behaviour and social life # Moves by fin flapping, jet propulsion and web expansion. Adaptations # Ear-like fins No ink sac (useless in darkness) Conservation # Vulnerable to bottom-trawling damage. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimpoteuthis WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Genus%20Grimpoteuthis FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Genus%20Grimpoteuthis

d: The largest octopus species, known for problem-solving and devoted, fatal motherhood.
x: Overview # Highly intelligent and able to recognise individual humans in aquaria. Each arm has ~280 suckers. Habitat and type of water # North Pacific coasts from Japan to California, intertidal to ~2,000 m. Feeding and hunting # Forages at night, drilling or prying open shellfish and leaving shell middens outside its den. Mating and reproduction # The male passes sperm with a modified arm (hectocotylus). The female lays up to ~100,000 eggs in a den and guards them without eating for ~6 months, then dies. Movement and migration # Moves to deeper water in winter in some regions. Behaviour and social life # Solitary, den-living, masters of camouflage. Adaptations # Colour-changing chromatophores Distributed nervous system with neurons in the arms Conservation # Targeted by small fisheries. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_Pacific_octopus WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Enteroctopus%20dofleini FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Enteroctopus%20dofleini

d: The source of kraken legends. First filmed alive in its deep habitat in 2012 and again in 2019 using a glowing lure.
x: Overview # Architeuthis has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom (~27 cm), likely for spotting the bioluminescent wakes of approaching sperm whales. Habitat and type of water # Worldwide, especially around New Zealand, Japan, the North Atlantic and southern Africa, 300–1,000 m. Feeding and hunting # Hunts fish and squid, seizing prey with two long feeding tentacles lined with toothed suckers. Mating and reproduction # Males have a long muscular penis and inject sperm packets into the female’s arms. Eggs are probably released in gelatinous masses. Movement and migration # Not well known. Behaviour and social life # Solitary. A key prey of sperm whales, which bear sucker scars from fights. Adaptations # Giant eyes Ammonium-rich tissues for buoyancy Toothed sucker rings Conservation # Not fished commercially. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_squid WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Architeuthis%20dux FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Architeuthis%20dux

d: Neither squid nor octopus: a gentle detritus eater living in the oxygen minimum zone.
x: Overview # The sole surviving member of its order. Despite its name it is not predatory: it collects marine snow with two retractile filaments and mucus. Habitat and type of water # Tropical and temperate oceans in oxygen minimum zones, 600–1,200 m. Feeding and hunting # Gathers sinking organic particles with sticky filaments and rolls them into mucus balls to eat. Mating and reproduction # Unusually for cephalopods, it appears to spawn multiple times over its life, with resting phases between. Movement and migration # Stays within the oxygen minimum zone, where few predators can follow. Behaviour and social life # When threatened it turns its webbed cloak inside out (‘pineapple posture’) and ejects glowing mucus instead of ink. Adaptations # Haemocyanin that binds oxygen efficiently in low-oxygen water Very low metabolic rate Bioluminescent arm tips Conservation # Not threatened. Expanding oxygen minimum zones may change its habitat. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire_squid WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Vampyroteuthis%20infernalis FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Vampyroteuthis%20infernalis

d: A deep-red crown jelly famous for its 'burglar alarm' display of spinning blue light.
x: Overview # When attacked, Atolla produces a ring of pulsing blue light that may attract larger predators to attack its attacker. This idea inspired the ‘Electronic Jellyfish’ lure that filmed the giant squid in 2012. Habitat and type of water # Worldwide in the midnight zone. Feeding and hunting # Captures small crustaceans with one elongated trailing tentacle. Mating and reproduction # Alternates between polyp and medusa stages like other scyphozoans (life cycle poorly known). Movement and migration # Drifts. Behaviour and social life # Bioluminescent ‘burglar alarm’. Adaptations # Red pigment invisible in deep blue light Defensive bioluminescence Conservation # Not threatened. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atolla_wyvillei WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Atolla%20wyvillei FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Atolla%20wyvillei

d: Reef-building coral that thrives in dark, cold water without symbiotic algae.
x: Overview # Deep-water reefs off Norway, Ireland and the US south-east host high biodiversity. Some deep corals, such as black corals, have lived over 4,000 years. Habitat and type of water # Continental margins, seamounts and fjords, mostly 200–1,000 m. Feeding and hunting # Catches zooplankton and particles from currents. It lacks the sunlight-dependent algae of tropical corals. Mating and reproduction # Separate sexes; broadcast spawns. Larvae can travel far on currents. Movement and migration # Sessile. Larvae disperse. Behaviour and social life # Grows slowly (mm to cm per year). Adaptations # No photosynthetic symbionts Long-lived colonies Conservation # Severely damaged by bottom trawling, and threatened by ocean acidification shoaling the aragonite saturation horizon. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmophyllum_pertusum WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Desmophyllum%20pertusum FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Desmophyllum%20pertusum

d: A colonial organism that rivals the blue whale in length, made of specialised zooids.
x: Overview # Siphonophores are colonies of clones (zooids) specialised for swimming, feeding or reproduction. In 2020, a spiralling Apolemia colony estimated at ~45 m was filmed off Western Australia. Habitat and type of water # Mid-water worldwide. Feeding and hunting # Sets a curtain of stinging tentacles and passively fishes. Mating and reproduction # Colonies reproduce sexually via specialised reproductive zooids, and grow by budding. Movement and migration # Drifts, with slow swimming. Behaviour and social life # Bioluminescent. Adaptations # Division of labour among zooids Conservation # Not threatened. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siphonophorae WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Praya%20dubia FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Praya%20dubia

d: Animals that partner with algae to build the largest biological structures on Earth.
x: Overview # Tropical corals host photosynthetic dinoflagellates (zooxanthellae) that supply most of their energy. Reefs cover under 1% of the seafloor but support roughly a quarter of marine species. Habitat and type of water # Shallow tropical seas; mesophotic reefs to ~150 m. Feeding and hunting # Gets sugars from symbionts. Hunts plankton at night with tentacles. Mating and reproduction # Many species broadcast spawn in mass synchronised events after full moons. Others brood larvae. Movement and migration # Sessile. Larvae disperse for days to weeks. Behaviour and social life # Bleach (expel symbionts) under heat stress. Adaptations # Algal symbiosis Calcium carbonate skeleton Conservation # The 4th global bleaching event (2023–25) hit 84.4% of reef area. Acidification and pollution add stress. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scleractinia WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Order%20Scleractinia%20(zooxanthellate) FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Order%20Scleractinia%20(zooxanthellate)

d: Possibly the most abundant wild animal by biomass (hundreds of millions of tonnes), and the base of the Antarctic food web.
x: Overview # Swarms can reach thousands of individuals per cubic metre. Whales, seals, penguins and fish depend on them. Habitat and type of water # Southern Ocean, mostly near the surface but recorded on the seafloor at ~4,000 m. Feeding and hunting # Filter-feeds on phytoplankton with a feeding basket and scrapes algae from under sea ice in winter. Mating and reproduction # Females spawn thousands of eggs that sink deep before hatching. Larvae swim up while developing. Movement and migration # Daily vertical migration, plus seasonal movements tied to sea ice. Behaviour and social life # Forms massive swarms. Can shrink in size when starved. Adaptations # Bioluminescent organs Ability to shrink when food is scarce Conservation # Growing commercial krill fishery and sea-ice loss are the main concerns. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_krill WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Euphausia%20superba FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Euphausia%20superba

d: A deep-sea relative of the woodlouse that can survive years between meals.
x: Overview # Deep-sea gigantism makes this isopod dozens of times bigger than its shallow relatives. One in captivity went more than five years without eating. Habitat and type of water # Western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean, on soft muddy bottoms. Feeding and hunting # Scavenger that gorges on food falls, and also takes slow live prey. Mating and reproduction # Females brood eggs in a pouch (marsupium). Young hatch as miniature adults. Movement and migration # Roams the seabed. Behaviour and social life # Rolls into a ball when threatened. Adaptations # Deep-sea gigantism Extreme fasting ability Conservation # Not threatened. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathynomus_giganteus WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Bathynomus%20giganteus FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Bathynomus%20giganteus

d: The largest arthropod by leg span.
x: Overview # Decorates its shell with sponges and algae for camouflage. Habitat and type of water # Waters around Japan. Feeding and hunting # Slow scavenger and forager. Mating and reproduction # Migrates to shallower water (~50 m) in spring to spawn. Females release up to ~1.5 million eggs. Movement and migration # Seasonal vertical migration for spawning. Behaviour and social life # Slow-moving. Moulting is risky at its size. Adaptations # Enormous legs Camouflage decoration Conservation # Fished. Spring spawning closures protect it. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_spider_crab WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Macrocheira%20kaempferi FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Macrocheira%20kaempferi

d: A hairy vent crab that farms chemosynthetic bacteria on its arms.
x: Overview # Discovered in 2005 at hydrothermal vents on the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge. It belongs to a family of its own (Kiwaidae). Habitat and type of water # Hydrothermal vents of the South Pacific. Feeding and hunting # ‘Dances’ its hairy claws in vent fluid to supply bacteria with oxygen and sulfide, then eats the bacteria. Mating and reproduction # Females may move away from hot vents to brood eggs in cooler water. Movement and migration # Clusters at vent margins. Behaviour and social life # Rhythmic arm-waving. Adaptations # Bacteria-farming setae Conservation # Vent habitats are potential targets for seabed mining. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwa_hirsuta WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Kiwa%20hirsuta FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Kiwa%20hirsuta

d: A fish with a transparent, fluid-filled head and tubular eyes that can rotate to look up through it.
x: Overview # First filmed alive by MBARI in 2004. The barreleye’s green ‘eyes’ are tubes inside a clear dome, and the spots above its mouth are actually its nostrils. Habitat and type of water # Subarctic to temperate North Pacific (Bering Sea to Baja California), twilight zone ~600–800 m. Feeding and hunting # Hangs nearly motionless looking upward for silhouettes. Researchers suspect it steals food from siphonophore tentacles, with the shield protecting its eyes from stinging cells. Mating and reproduction # Poorly known. Thought to broadcast spawn pelagic eggs. Movement and migration # Not known to migrate far vertically. Behaviour and social life # Hovers with large fins and rotates its eyes from upward to forward to track prey into its mouth. d: The classic deep-sea anglerfish: a lure of glowing bacteria, a cavernous mouth and dwarf males.
x: Overview # A black, globe-shaped predator of the bathypelagic zone and one of the most recognisable deep-sea animals. Habitat and type of water # Open water of the midnight zone worldwide in tropical to temperate seas, mostly 1,000–2,000 m, recorded from ~200 to ~4,500 m. Feeding and hunting # A sit-and-wait ambush predator. It hangs motionless and wiggles its glowing lure to draw prey close, then engulfs it. Its stomach and jaws expand so it can swallow prey as large as itself, which matters where meals are rare. Mating and reproduction # Males are tiny and free-swimming, with large nostrils for tracking female pheromones. In Melanocetus the male attaches temporarily to the female; in some other anglerfish families males fuse permanently (sexual parasitism). Eggs are released in buoyant gelatinous veils, and larvae develop in shallower water. Movement and migration # Larvae and juveniles live higher in the water column and descend as they mature (ontogenetic migration). Adults do not migrate daily. Behaviour and social life # Solitary, energy-saving and largely motionless. Encounters between the sexes are rare, which is why mate-finding adaptations are so extreme. Adaptations # Bacterial bioluminescent lure Distensible stomach and hinged jaws Black, light-absorbing skin Weak, watery muscles that save energy Conservation # Not commercially fished. d: Possibly the most abundant vertebrates on Earth; their nightly migration is the largest on the planet.
x: Overview # About 250 species of small fish covered in photophores (light organs) in species-specific patterns. Together they may make up a large share of the global fish biomass, and they underpin food webs for tuna, squid, seabirds and marine mammals. Habitat and type of water # Every ocean, mesopelagic zone by day (300–1,500 m), near-surface by night. Feeding and hunting # Feed at night near the surface on copepods, krill and other zooplankton, then descend at dawn to digest in dark, cold water safe from visual predators. Mating and reproduction # Broadcast spawners with pelagic eggs and larvae. Many species mature within a year, and their short lives support rapid population turnover. Movement and migration # Diel vertical migration: hundreds of metres up at dusk and down at dawn, every day. This transports carbon to depth (the ‘migrant pump’). Behaviour and social life # Schooling. Photophores on the belly provide counter-illumination, matching downwelling light to hide the fish’s silhouette from predators below. Adaptations # Ventral photophores for counter-illumination Large eyes tuned to blue light Gas-filled or lipid-filled swim bladders (varies by species) Conservation # Targeted by small experimental fisheries for fishmeal. Scientists caution that large-scale twilight-zone fishing could weaken the ocean’s carbon pump. x: Overview # Can fly thousands of kilometres with barely a wing flap. Habitat and type of water # Southern Ocean. Feeding and hunting # Seizes squid at the surface, often at night. Mating and reproduction # Breeds every two years. Lifelong pair bonds. Movement and migration # Circumpolar foraging trips. Behaviour and social life # Elaborate courtship dances. Adaptations # Shoulder lock for gliding Salt glands Conservation # Longline bycatch is the main threat. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wandering_albatross WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Diomedea%20exulans FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Diomedea%20exulans

d: An eel-like shark with 300 needle teeth, often called a living fossil.
x: Overview # Named for its six frilly gill slits. Its body plan resembles fossil sharks from hundreds of millions of years ago. Habitat and type of water # Outer continental shelves and slopes, patchily worldwide. Feeding and hunting # May strike like a snake, bending its body back and lunging. Its many inward-facing teeth trap slippery squid. Mating and reproduction # Ovoviviparous, with the longest gestation recorded in any vertebrate: possibly up to 3.5 years. Movement and migration # Undertakes vertical movements. Behaviour and social life # Rarely observed alive. Adaptations # Trident-shaped teeth Flexible eel-like body Conservation # Low reproductive rate makes it sensitive to bycatch. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frilled_shark WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Chlamydoselachus%20anguineus FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Chlamydoselachus%20anguineus

d: The largest ray, with the largest brain-to-body ratio of any fish, and dives deep into the twilight zone.
x: Overview # Mantas visit ‘cleaning stations’ on reefs and may recognise themselves in mirrors, an area of active study. Habitat and type of water # Tropical to temperate oceans, around oceanic islands and productive coasts. Feeding and hunting # Filter-feeds, sometimes by somersaulting repeatedly through plankton patches. Deep dives suggest they also feed on mesopelagic plankton. Mating and reproduction # Gives birth to one pup every 2–5 years after a ~1-year gestation, one of the lowest reproductive rates of any fish. Movement and migration # Seasonal migrations tied to plankton productivity. Behaviour and social life # Curious, sometimes approaching divers. Uses cleaning stations. Adaptations # Cephalic fins that funnel water Large brain with a rete mirabile for warming Conservation # Gill plates are traded internationally. Listed on CITES Appendix II. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_oceanic_manta_ray WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Mobula%20birostris FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Mobula%20birostris

d: Its jaws catapult forward at high speed to snatch prey, one of the fastest jaw projections among sharks.
x: Overview # A pinkish, soft-bodied shark with a long flattened snout covered in electroreceptors. Habitat and type of water # Continental slopes and seamounts worldwide, most records from Japan. Feeding and hunting # Detects prey electrically, then ‘slingshots’ its jaws forward to grab it. Mating and reproduction # Reproduction is little known; presumed ovoviviparous like its relatives. Movement and migration # Juveniles are sometimes found in shallower submarine canyons. Behaviour and social life # Slow, neutrally buoyant swimmer. Adaptations # Protrusible slingshot jaws Ampullae of Lorenzini on the snout Conservation # Rare bycatch. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_shark WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Mitsukurina%20owstoni FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Mitsukurina%20owstoni

d: Apex predator famous for ocean-crossing migrations and dives into the twilight zone.
x: Overview # The largest predatory fish. Partly warm-blooded (regionally endothermic), so it can hunt in cold water. Habitat and type of water # Coastal and offshore temperate waters worldwide, with dives regularly reaching hundreds of metres. Feeding and hunting # Ambushes seals from below with high-speed vertical attacks, and scavenges whale carcasses. Mating and reproduction # Ovoviviparous with intrauterine cannibalism (oophagy). Matures late (females ~33 years). Movement and migration # Long migrations, e.g. between California and the ‘White Shark Café’ mid-Pacific, or South Africa to Australia. Behaviour and social life # Investigates objects by biting. Social hierarchies observed at feeding sites. Adaptations # Regional endothermy Acute electroreception and smell Conservation # Protected in many countries. Threatened by bycatch and historic trophy hunting. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Carcharodon%20carcharias FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Carcharodon%20carcharias

d: The longest-lived vertebrate known: radiocarbon dating of eye lenses suggests ages of several centuries.
x: Overview # A massive, slow-moving sleeper shark of Arctic and North Atlantic waters. A 2016 study dated one individual at roughly 392 ± 120 years. Habitat and type of water # Arctic and North Atlantic, from the surface in winter to over 2,000 m. Feeding and hunting # Opportunistic feeder on fish, seals (possibly caught while asleep) and carrion, including drowned reindeer and polar bear remains. Mating and reproduction # Ovoviviparous. Females may not reach maturity until ~150 years old. Movement and migration # Moves vertically and seasonally. Tagging shows long-distance movements. Behaviour and social life # Swims extremely slowly (around 1 km/h). Many have copepod parasites attached to their eyes. Adaptations # Cold-adapted slow metabolism Urea and TMAO-rich tissues Conservation # Bycatch in Arctic fisheries is a concern for a species that reproduces so late. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Somniosus%20microcephalus FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Somniosus%20microcephalus

d: The largest fish alive, a gentle filter feeder that dives to nearly 2 km.
x: Overview # Each whale shark has a unique spot pattern used for photo-identification by citizen scientists. Habitat and type of water # Tropical and warm-temperate seas. Aggregation sites include Ningaloo, Mexico, the Philippines and the Maldives. Feeding and hunting # Filter-feeds by ram feeding or active suction, timing visits to coral spawning and fish spawning events. Mating and reproduction # One pregnant female held about 300 embryos at different stages, which suggests sperm storage. Ovoviviparous. Movement and migration # Ocean-basin-scale migrations. Dives below 1,900 m have been recorded. Behaviour and social life # Usually solitary but gathers seasonally at food-rich sites. Adaptations # Gill rakers that filter plankton Thick skin up to ~10 cm Conservation # Endangered due to fisheries, bycatch and ship strikes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_shark WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Rhincodon%20typus FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Rhincodon%20typus

d: A glass sponge whose silica lattice inspires engineers, and a lifelong home for a pair of shrimp.
x: Overview # Its skeleton of fused silica spicules is extraordinarily strong. A male and female shrimp enter as larvae and grow too big to leave, living out their lives inside. Habitat and type of water # Western Pacific and Indian Ocean. Feeding and hunting # Filters bacteria and particles from water flowing through its body. Mating and reproduction # Can reproduce sexually or by budding. Movement and migration # Sessile. Behaviour and social life # Long-lived. Its fibre-optic-like spicules transmit light. Adaptations # Silica skeleton Conservation # Vulnerable to trawling. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus%2527_flower_basket WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Euplectella%20aspergillum FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Euplectella%20aspergillum

d: Mouthless worms that bore into whale bones using acid and live off bacteria.
x: Overview # Osedax females drill into whale (and other vertebrate) bones with root-like tissue that secretes acid. Microscopic dwarf males live inside the female’s tube. Habitat and type of water # Whale falls and other bones on the seafloor worldwide. Feeding and hunting # Symbiotic bacteria in the roots digest collagen and lipids from bone. Mating and reproduction # Dozens of dwarf males live in the female’s tube and fertilise her eggs. Larvae disperse to find new bones. Movement and migration # Larvae must find rare, scattered food falls. Behaviour and social life # Colonies of red plumes cover bones within months of a whale’s arrival. Adaptations # Acid-secreting roots Dwarf males Conservation # Fewer whales means fewer whale falls. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osedax WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Genus%20Osedax FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Genus%20Osedax

d: The most numerous animals in deep-sea sediments, found even at the bottom of the Challenger Deep.
x: Overview # Meiofauna are animals between 0.03 and 1 mm living between sediment grains. Nematode worms dominate, often millions per square metre. Habitat and type of water # Sediments from beaches to hadal trenches. Feeding and hunting # Graze bacteria and detritus, recycling nutrients in sediments. Mating and reproduction # Short generation times and diverse reproductive modes. Movement and migration # Mostly sedentary within sediments. Behaviour and social life # Their communities are used as indicators of disturbance, including mining impacts. Adaptations # Tiny size Tolerance of low oxygen Conservation # Directly affected by trawling and mining that disturb sediments. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiobenthos WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Mostly%20phylum%20Nematoda FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Mostly%20phylum%20Nematoda

d: The icon of hydrothermal vents: a mouthless, gutless worm fed entirely by internal bacteria.
x: Overview # Riftia was discovered at the Galápagos Rift after vents were found in 1977. It has no mouth or gut as an adult; a spongy organ (trophosome) holds billions of sulfur-oxidising bacteria. Habitat and type of water # East Pacific Rise and Galápagos Rift hydrothermal vents. Feeding and hunting # Its red plume absorbs oxygen, CO₂ and hydrogen sulfide. A special haemoglobin carries the sulfide to its bacteria, which make sugars for the worm. Mating and reproduction # Separate sexes. Sperm bundles fertilise eggs released into the water. Larvae (which do have a gut) pick up bacteria from the environment. Movement and migration # Larvae disperse along the ridge to colonise new vents. Behaviour and social life # Among the fastest-growing invertebrates, able to grow over 85 cm a year. Adaptations # Sulfide-binding haemoglobin Trophosome housing symbionts Conservation # Vents are ephemeral and could be affected by seafloor massive sulfide mining. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftia_pachyptila WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Riftia%20pachyptila FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Riftia%20pachyptila

d: One of the most heat-tolerant complex animals, living in tubes on black-smoker chimneys.
x: Overview # Covered by a fleece of bacteria on its back that may insulate it. Its tube can have temperatures above 60 °C at one end. Habitat and type of water # East Pacific Rise vent chimneys. Feeding and hunting # Grazes bacteria and may farm its epibiotic bacteria. Mating and reproduction # Internal fertilisation has been suggested. Embryos develop best at cooler temperatures (~10 °C). Movement and migration # Sessile in tubes. Behaviour and social life # Secretes mucus that may feed its bacterial partners. Adaptations # Heat-stable proteins Symbiotic bacterial fleece Conservation # Vent mining is a potential threat. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii_worm WoRMS search: https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxlist&tName=Alvinella%20pompejana FishBase / SeaLifeBase search: https://www.fishbase.se/Nomenclature/ScientificNameSearchList.php?crit1_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynGenus&crit1_fieldtype=CHAR&crit1_operator=EQUAL&crit2_fieldname=SYNONYMS.SynSpecies&crit2_fieldtype=CHAR&crit2_operator=EQUAL&group=summary&backstep=-2&gs=Alvinella%20pompejana

d: The largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of Earth's surface.
x: Overview # Larger than all land combined. Ringed by the ‘Ring of Fire’ of subduction zones, volcanoes and the deepest trenches. Geography and seafloor # Bounded by Asia and Australia to the west and the Americas to the east. Holds the Mariana, Tonga, Kuril–Kamchatka, Philippine and Kermadec trenches. Water, currents and climate # The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) in the tropical Pacific drives global climate variability. It holds the largest oxygen minimum zones (eastern tropical Pacific). Flora and fauna # The Coral Triangle (the world’s peak marine biodiversity), the Clarion-Clipperton Zone nodule fields, and hadal snailfish. People and economy # The largest tuna fisheries. Island nations depend heavily on it. Threats and protection # Deep-sea mining in the CCZ, warming, bleaching, plastics (the Great Pacific Garbage Patch). Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Pacific%20Ocean

d: The second-largest ocean, split down the middle by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and home to the AMOC.
x: Overview # An S-shaped basin widening by a few cm a year along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Geography and seafloor # Between the Americas and Europe/Africa. Includes the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Mediterranean and North Sea as marginal seas. Water, currents and climate # The Gulf Stream and AMOC carry heat north. The North Atlantic is a key site of deep-water formation. Flora and fauna # Lost City hydrothermal field, the Sargasso Sea (eel spawning), cold-water coral reefs. People and economy # Historic cod, herring and tuna fisheries. Major shipping lanes. Threats and protection # AMOC weakening, overfishing, hurricanes intensified by warm water. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Atlantic%20Ocean

d: The warmest ocean, ruled by monsoon reversals of winds and currents.
x: Overview # Enclosed to the north by Asia, so it lacks a northern polar connection. Geography and seafloor # Between Africa, Asia, Australia and the Southern Ocean. Includes the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Water, currents and climate # Monsoon-driven seasonal current reversal (Somali Current). The Indian Ocean Dipole affects rainfall in India, Africa and Australia. Flora and fauna # Coelacanths, whale sharks of the Maldives, scaly-foot snails at vents. People and economy # Crucial for Indian, East African and Indonesian fisheries and trade. Threats and protection # Fastest-warming ocean, bleaching, oxygen loss in the Arabian Sea. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Indian%20Ocean

d: The ring of ocean around Antarctica, driven by the strongest current on Earth.
x: Overview # Recognised as the fifth ocean by the IHO in 2000 and by National Geographic in 2021. Geography and seafloor # South of ~60°S around Antarctica. Water, currents and climate # The Antarctic Circumpolar Current moves ~100+ million m³/s. It forms Antarctic Bottom Water and takes up a large share of anthropogenic heat and CO₂. Flora and fauna # Krill, penguins, colossal squid, Antarctic toothfish, icefish (with no haemoglobin). People and economy # Managed by CCAMLR. Krill and toothfish fisheries. Threats and protection # Sea-ice loss, warming, acidification, krill fishing. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Southern%20Ocean

d: The smallest, shallowest ocean, losing its summer sea ice fast.
x: Overview # Surrounded by Eurasia and North America, with wide continental shelves. Geography and seafloor # Connected to the Atlantic via the Fram Strait and to the Pacific via the Bering Strait. Water, currents and climate # A fresh, cold surface layer over warmer Atlantic water. Summer sea-ice extent has fallen sharply since 1979. Flora and fauna # Narwhals, belugas, polar bears, Greenland sharks. People and economy # New shipping routes and resource interest as ice retreats. Threats and protection # Ice loss, ‘Atlantification’, pollution transported from lower latitudes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Arctic%20Ocean

d: A nearly enclosed sea with unusually warm, salty deep water and a long human history.
x: Overview # Connected to the Atlantic by the 14 km-wide Strait of Gibraltar. It nearly dried out during the Messinian salinity crisis (~5.9–5.3 million years ago). Geography and seafloor # Between Europe, North Africa and Western Asia. Water, currents and climate # Evaporation exceeds inflow, so it is very salty. Deep water stays ~13 °C, much warmer than most of the deep ocean. Flora and fauna # Posidonia seagrass meadows, monk seals, bluefin tuna spawning grounds. A biodiversity hotspot with many endemics. People and economy # Over 150 million coastal inhabitants and heavy tourism. Threats and protection # Marine heatwaves, invasive species via the Suez Canal, overfishing, plastics. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Mediterranean%20Sea

d: A tropical sea of coral reefs and the deepest point of the Caribbean, the Cayman Trough.
x: Overview # Bounded by the Antilles island arcs and Central/South America. Geography and seafloor # Contains the Mesoamerican Reef, the second-largest barrier reef system. Water, currents and climate # Warm surface waters fuel Atlantic hurricanes. Flora and fauna # Reef fish, sea turtles, invasive lionfish, the world’s deepest known vents (Beebe vent field, ~5,000 m). People and economy # Tourism and fisheries economies. Threats and protection # Bleaching, Sargassum influxes, invasive lionfish. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Caribbean%20Sea

d: A basin of natural oil seeps, brine pools and a large seasonal 'dead zone'.
x: Overview # Partly enclosed by the US, Mexico and Cuba. Geography and seafloor # Fed by the Loop Current and the Mississippi River. Water, currents and climate # Nutrient runoff from the Mississippi creates a large hypoxic zone each summer. Flora and fauna # Brine pools with ‘hot tub of despair’ lakes, cold seeps, giant isopods. People and economy # Major oil and gas region. Deepwater Horizon spill in 2010. Threats and protection # Hypoxia, oil pollution, intensifying hurricanes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Gulf%20of%20Mexico

d: The only sea without coastlines, defined by currents and floating Sargassum seaweed.
x: Overview # Bounded by the currents of the North Atlantic Gyre. Geography and seafloor # Mid-North Atlantic around Bermuda. Water, currents and climate # Calm, clear and warm. Sargassum mats float at the surface. Flora and fauna # The spawning ground of European and American eels, and a nursery for turtles. People and economy # Hamilton Declaration (2014) for conservation cooperation. Threats and protection # Plastic accumulation in the gyre, shipping. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Sargasso%20Sea

d: A shallow, heavily used shelf sea between Britain and mainland Europe.
x: Overview # Formed over a drowned landscape (Doggerland) flooded after the last ice age. Geography and seafloor # Between the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Water, currents and climate # Shallow and well-mixed, with strong tides. Flora and fauna # Herring, cod, harbour porpoises, grey seals. People and economy # Oil and gas, the largest offshore wind build-out in the world, shipping. Threats and protection # Bottom trawling (high carbon disturbance), heavy shipping. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=North%20Sea

d: A young brackish sea with some of the largest dead zones on Earth.
x: Overview # Formed after the last glaciation and still rising due to post-glacial rebound. Geography and seafloor # Enclosed by Scandinavia, the Baltic states, Poland, Germany, Russia and Finland. Water, currents and climate # A low-salinity surface over a salty, often anoxic deep layer. Flora and fauna # Few species tolerate brackish water. Grey seals, cod (in decline). People and economy # Shipping and fishing. Threats and protection # Eutrophication and hypoxia, overfishing. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Baltic%20Sea

d: The largest anoxic body of water on Earth: below ~150–200 m there is no oxygen.
x: Overview # A meromictic sea: the layers never mix fully. Geography and seafloor # Between Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Anatolia, linked to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus. Water, currents and climate # Hydrogen-sulfide-rich deep water preserves ancient shipwrecks remarkably well. Flora and fauna # Life mostly confined to the upper ~150 m. Dolphins, anchovy. People and economy # Fisheries and strategic shipping. Threats and protection # Eutrophication, invasive comb jellies (historic), conflict. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Black%20Sea

d: A young ocean in the making, with heat-tolerant corals and hot brine pools.
x: Overview # Africa and Arabia are rifting apart here. Geography and seafloor # Between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula; connected to the Indian Ocean (Bab-el-Mandeb) and the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal. Water, currents and climate # Very salty and warm. Deep water stays ~21 °C. Flora and fauna # Corals unusually tolerant of heat, brine-pool microbes. People and economy # One of the busiest shipping routes (Suez). Threats and protection # Coastal development, shipping disruption. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Red%20Sea

d: Home to one of the world's thickest oxygen minimum zones, driven by monsoon upwelling.
x: Overview # Bounded by India, Pakistan, Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. Geography and seafloor # North-western Indian Ocean. Water, currents and climate # Summer monsoon upwelling drives huge productivity and a deep oxygen minimum zone. Flora and fauna # Lanternfish swarms, whale sharks, the Arabian humpback whale (a resident, isolated population). People and economy # Fisheries and shipping to the Gulf. Threats and protection # Expanding low-oxygen zones, cyclones intensified by warming. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Arabian%20Sea

d: The world's largest bay, freshened by the Ganges–Brahmaputra and fuelling strong cyclones.
x: Overview # Receives enormous river discharge and sediment (the Bengal Fan, the largest submarine fan). Geography and seafloor # Bounded by India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Water, currents and climate # A freshwater lid causes strong stratification, which favours cyclone intensification. Flora and fauna # Mangrove Sundarbans, Irrawaddy dolphins, olive ridley turtle mass nesting (arribadas in Odisha). People and economy # Dense coastal populations and fisheries. Threats and protection # Cyclones, sea-level rise, oxygen minimum zone. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Bay%20of%20Bengal

d: Home to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth.
x: Overview # Off north-east Australia. Geography and seafloor # Between Australia, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu. Water, currents and climate # Warm tropical waters. Flora and fauna # The Great Barrier Reef (~2,300 km). The Ocean Census found many new species here in 2025–26. People and economy # Tourism and a protected marine park. Threats and protection # Repeated mass bleaching (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024). Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Coral%20Sea

d: A biodiverse and contested sea crossed by a large share of global shipping.
x: Overview # Bounded by China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Geography and seafloor # Western Pacific marginal sea. Water, currents and climate # Monsoon-driven circulation. Flora and fauna # Extensive reefs (Spratlys, Paracels) and large fisheries. People and economy # A major trade route. x: Overview # Between Alaska and Russia, connecting to the Arctic via the Bering Strait. Geography and seafloor # North Pacific. x: Overview # Off the Antarctic Peninsula and Coats Land. Geography and seafloor # Southern Ocean. Water, currents and climate # Brine rejection from sea ice forms some of the densest water on Earth. d: Often called the most pristine marine ecosystem left, and protected by a large MPA since 2017.
x: Overview # A deep bay of the Southern Ocean beside the Ross Ice Shelf. Geography and seafloor # Antarctica. Water, currents and climate # Polynyas drive high productivity. d: A hot, hyper-saline shallow sea whose corals survive extremes that kill corals elsewhere.
x: Overview # Between the Arabian Peninsula and Iran. Geography and seafloor # Indian Ocean (via the Strait of Hormuz). Water, currents and climate # Summer surface temperatures above 35 °C.
